broadcastId.label: Broadcast ID
broadcastId.tooltip: A short code that uniquely identifies this broadcast. Your AV technician will find it in the broadcast equipment's settings. It uses only numbers and the letters A–F (for example: 1A2B or FF003C). It can be 1–6 characters long.

deviceAddress.label: Device Address
deviceAddress.tooltip: The Bluetooth hardware address of your broadcast transmitter — similar to a serial number for the device. Your AV technician can find it in the device's settings menu or on a sticker on the equipment itself. It looks like AA:BB:CC:00:11:22. You can leave this blank if you're unsure.

addressType.label: Address Type
addressType.tooltip: Describes how your broadcast device identifies itself over Bluetooth. 'Public' means it uses a fixed, permanent address — the most common setting for venue equipment. 'Random' means the address changes periodically for privacy. If in doubt, choose Public or ask your AV technician.

audioQuality.label: Audio Quality
audioQuality.tooltip: Indicates the audio quality levels your broadcast supports. 'Standard' (SQ) works on most Auracast-compatible devices. 'High' (HQ) delivers better audio but requires newer receivers. Choose 'Both' if your equipment transmits both quality levels simultaneously. Check your broadcast equipment's documentation if you're unsure — or ask your AV technician.

encrypted.label: Encrypted broadcast
encrypted.tooltip: Tick this if your broadcast is password-protected. Encrypted broadcasts require listeners to enter a code before they can tune in. The code is set on your broadcast equipment — ask your AV technician for it before enabling this option.

broadcastCode.label: Broadcast Code
broadcastCode.tooltip: The password listeners need to access your encrypted broadcast. This code is configured on your broadcast equipment — your AV technician will be able to provide it. It can be up to 16 characters long.

advertisingSid.label: Advertising SID
advertisingSid.tooltip: The Advertising Set Identifier of the broadcast's periodic advertising. Some receivers — notably certain hearing aids — need it to lock onto the stream. Your AV technician will find it in the broadcast equipment's settings. It's a single number from 0 to 15.

paInterval.label: Periodic Advertising Interval
paInterval.tooltip: How often the broadcaster sends its periodic advertising, in hexadecimal. Some receivers use it to sync faster. Your AV technician will find it in the broadcast equipment's settings. Leave blank if you're unsure.

preview.title: QR Preview
preview.placeholder: Enter a Broadcast Name (min 4 chars) to see your QR code

centreImage.label: Image
centreImage.warning: Custom images are not included in the shareable URL — collaborators will need to re-upload.

meta.title: What is Auracast? Bluetooth Broadcast Audio Explained
meta.description: Learn how Auracast Bluetooth broadcast audio works — who it helps, where it's deployed, and why it's transforming hearing accessibility in public spaces.

hero.heading: What is Auracast?
hero.p1: Auracast is a Bluetooth broadcast audio standard developed by the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG). It lets a single device — a TV, PA system, or dedicated transmitter — stream audio to an unlimited number of nearby listeners simultaneously, without any pairing or setup required on the listener’s end.
hero.p2: Think of it like a local radio station, but delivered over Bluetooth. Anyone with a compatible device can tune in just by being within range.

difference.heading: How is it different from regular Bluetooth?
difference.p: Standard Bluetooth is designed for private, one-to-one connections — your phone to your earbuds, for example. Each connection is exclusive and paired. Auracast works the opposite way: it broadcasts audio outward like a public signal, and any number of compatible devices can receive it at the same time.

who.heading: Who does Auracast help?
who.p: Auracast was built with accessibility at its core. While anyone can use it, it has the most transformative impact for people who rely on hearing technology.

cards.heading: Hearing aid and cochlear implant users
cards.body: Modern hearing aids and cochlear implants are increasingly Bluetooth LE Audio compatible. Auracast lets them stream crystal-clear audio directly from a venue’s sound system — cutting out background noise entirely.

cards.heading: Anyone in a noisy environment
cards.body: Crowded airports, busy stations, or echoing halls are hard for everyone. Auracast delivers audio straight to the listener, bypassing the acoustic chaos of the room.

cards.heading: Multilingual audiences
cards.body: A single room can broadcast on multiple Auracast channels simultaneously — one per language. Attendees select their preferred stream without any physical equipment handout.

where.heading: Where is Auracast being used?
where.p: Auracast is designed for any public space where audio matters. Early deployments are appearing in:

venues.heading: Airports & transport hubs
venues.desc: Gate announcements streamed directly to passengers

venues.heading: Theatres & cinemas
venues.desc: Crystal-clear dialogue without a hearing loop receiver

venues.heading: Places of worship
venues.desc: Sermons and music delivered to every seat

qrCodes.heading: How do QR codes fit in?
qrCodes.p1: Finding the right Auracast broadcast in a busy venue can be tricky — just like picking the right Wi-Fi network from a long list. An Auracast QR code solves this instantly.
qrCodes.p2: A compatible device scans the code and connects directly to the correct broadcast — no scrolling, no guessing. The QR code encodes the broadcast’s name, its Bluetooth identifier, and optionally a security passcode for encrypted streams.
qrCodes.p3: Venues print these codes on seats, walls, programmes, or screens — the same way you’d display a Wi-Fi QR code.

cta.heading: Ready to create a code?
cta.subtext: Generate a SIG-compliant Auracast QR code in seconds.

meta.title: How Auracast QR Codes Work — URI Format Explained
meta.description: A plain-English guide to the Bluetooth URI inside every Auracast QR code — field by field, with worked examples and terminal commands for Base64 encoding.

hero.heading: How Auracast QR codes are generated
hero.p: Every Auracast QR code contains a specially formatted text string — a Bluetooth URI. This page walks through exactly what that string contains and how it is built, field by field.

atAGlance.heading: The URI at a glance
atAGlance.p: The string follows the Bluetooth SIG Auracast specification. Here is a complete example for a broadcast called “Airport” with a public Bluetooth address and a High Quality stream:
atAGlance.note: Each piece of information is separated by a semicolon. The string always ends with a double semicolon.

rows.label: Auracast service identifier
rows.description: This never changes. 184F is the Bluetooth SIG-assigned UUID for Public Broadcast Audio — it tells any scanning device that this QR code is for an Auracast broadcast, not a regular Bluetooth device.

rows.label: Broadcast Name
rows.description: The human-readable name of the broadcast, encoded in Base64. Base64 converts text into a safe sequence of printable characters so that any name — including accented letters or non-English characters — survives intact inside the URI. For example, the name “Airport” becomes QWlycG9ydA==. The == at the end is standard Base64 padding.

rows.label: Address Type
rows.description: Describes the kind of Bluetooth address the broadcaster is using. 0 means a public (permanent) address — the same every time. 1 means a random address, which some devices rotate for privacy. Only included in the URI when an Advertiser Address is also provided.

rows.label: Advertiser Address
rows.description: The Bluetooth MAC address of the broadcasting device, written as 12 uppercase hexadecimal characters with no colons. For example, A1:B2:C3:D4:E5:F6 becomes A1B2C3D4E5F6. Including this helps a receiver lock onto the exact broadcaster rather than any nearby device with the same name.

rows.label: Advertising SID
rows.description: The Advertising Set Identifier of the broadcaster's periodic advertising — a single number from 0 to 15. Some receivers, notably certain hearing aids, require it to establish sync with the stream. Only included when provided.

rows.label: Broadcast ID
rows.description: A unique identifier for the broadcast stream, written in hexadecimal (1 to 6 characters). This is assigned by the broadcaster and distinguishes it from other Auracast streams in the same area.
rows.note: Note: while the Broadcast ID is technically required by the Auracast specification, many real-world implementations omit it without issue. Most transmitters run only a single broadcast at a time, so receiver devices can identify the stream without an explicit ID — and popular platforms such as Google Pixel handle its absence gracefully. In practice, you'll frequently encounter working Auracast deployments where this field is not present.

rows.label: Periodic Advertising Interval
rows.description: The interval of the broadcaster's periodic advertising, written in hexadecimal (1 to 4 characters). It lets a receiver anticipate the next advertising packet and sync more efficiently. Only included when provided.

rows.label: Standard Quality stream
rows.description: Present only when the broadcast includes a Standard Quality audio stream. Standard Quality uses less bandwidth — useful for speech, announcements, or lower-power scenarios. If this stream is not available, the field is omitted entirely.

rows.label: High Quality stream
rows.description: Present only when the broadcast includes a High Quality audio stream. High Quality delivers richer, fuller sound — better for music, entertainment, or premium listening experiences. Both SQ:1 and HQ:1 can appear together if the broadcaster offers both.

rows.label: Broadcast Code
rows.description: Only present for encrypted broadcasts. This is the passcode a listener needs to access the audio, encoded in Base64. The raw passcode is padded to exactly 16 bytes before encoding, ensuring a consistent length. Without the correct code, a device can see the broadcast exists but cannot decrypt the audio.

base64.heading: Why Base64?
base64.p: The Auracast URI format uses semicolons as separators. If a broadcast name contained a semicolon, it would break the structure. Base64 solves this: it converts any text — including special characters, emoji, or non-English scripts — into a string that only uses the 64 safe characters A–Z a–z 0–9 + / plus optional = padding.
base64.notice: Notice how the accented é in “Café” is handled cleanly — the Base64 output looks nothing like the input, but it decodes back perfectly every time.

terminal.heading: Try it yourself in a terminal

linux.title: Linux — Terminal
linux.note: The commands are identical to macOS.

windows.title: Windows — PowerShell
windows.note: Windows doesn’t have a built-in base64 command, but PowerShell handles it natively. The extra step specifying UTF-8 ensures accented or non-English characters encode correctly.

terminal.flagNote: On macOS and Linux, the -n flag on echo is important — without it a trailing newline gets included in the encoding and the result will be wrong.

workedExample.heading: A worked example
workedExample.p: Let’s build the URI step by step for this broadcast:

steps.label: Start with the Auracast service identifier
steps.note: This prefix is fixed — it never changes.

steps.label: Append the Advertising SID
steps.note: AS:8 — required by some receivers to establish sync

steps.label: Append the Broadcast ID
steps.note: The unique hex identifier for this stream

steps.label: Append the Periodic Advertising Interval
steps.note: PI:FFFF — the periodic advertising interval, in hex

steps.label: Append the quality flag
steps.note: HQ:1 is added because High Quality is selected. SQ:1 is omitted.

steps.label: Close with a double semicolon
steps.note: The trailing ;; signals the end of the Auracast URI.

completeUri.heading: The complete URI
completeUri.p: This is the final string that gets embedded into the QR code. Any compatible Bluetooth device can scan it and connect directly to the broadcast.
completeUri.note: The QR code is generated from this string at the highest error-correction level available, so the code remains scannable even if part of it is obscured or damaged.
